From Skepticism to a Historic 9.90
How Puripon Boonson and Coach Gentry Bradley Struck Asian Games Gold
The weight training room at the Athletic Association of Thailand under Royal Patronage in Bangkok. BLACK DOT | PERSPECTIVE

BANGKOK — At just 20 years old, Thai sprint sensation Puripon Boonson has firmly etched his name into the track and field history books. Clocking a blistering 9.90 seconds, Boonson recently captured the 100-meter gold medal at the Asian Games, shattering the previous game record and breaking the highly coveted 10-second barrier. Yet, behind this monumental triumph lies an unlikely partnership forged in a humble Bangkok gym and a coaching philosophy built on mechanical precision and absolute patience.

The architect behind Boonson's refined stride is coach Gentry Bradley, who approaches sprinting with the meticulous eye of a master mechanic.

"You have to take the car and first find out what’s working, what’s good," Bradley explained regarding his analytical method. "Once we have that, now we have to see what’s bad, where we are not being efficient, where are we losing most of our power."

The road to the podium, however, began with a heavy dose of doubt. When Bradley first took the reins, the young prodigy was openly skeptical of his new mentor. Boonson had no prior knowledge of Bradley's coaching portfolio and had never seen the results he had produced with other athletes. Furthermore, Bradley’s own personal best as a runner was slower than the times Boonson was already clocking.

"It’s true, I didn’t know him before," Boonson admitted. "Personally, he was slower than me when he ran. So I wondered, can he really make me faster?"

That skepticism evaporated entirely the day Boonson finally broke the 10-second barrier and beat his own personal record. For Bradley, that breakthrough was the exact moment he knew his athlete had bought into the program. He realized that from that historic run onward, Boonson would believe in him 100 percent.

The cornerstone of Bradley’s training regimen is discipline over immediate speed. "Slow yourself down at the beginning. You have to be patient," Bradley advises his athletes. "Patience is the number one thing in sprinting. Understand the movement that you’re trying to do, and then get stronger and better in the movement. And then let your talent be added to the movement."

It is a two-way street of inspiration. Bradley notes that Boonson’s relentless will to win and his profound desire to be the absolute best constantly push him as a coach to elevate his own game. "This type of drive motivates a coach to try to do better," Bradley said. "It makes me ask: How can I help him run faster?"

Perhaps the most surprising element of Boonson's record-breaking gold is where the physical foundation was laid. The duo trains at the Athletic Association of Thailand under Royal Patronage in Bangkok. To an outside observer or a visiting guest, the weight training room and its equipment look decidedly dated, a stark contrast to the gleaming, state-of-the-art facilities typical of modern athletic superpowers.

But where others might see outdated gear, Boonson sees legacy and efficiency. Instead of demanding new resources, he utilizes his environment with remarkable effectiveness.

"Yeah, this place has been where many athletes have built themselves up, going all the way back to the legendary athletes," Boonson remarked when asked about the older equipment.

Rather than cycling through expensive new gear, the association has meticulously maintained a core segment of its older equipment. Keeping this seasoned equipment in active rotation is more than just a nod to the past; it serves as a masterclass in resource efficiency and zero-waste generation.

Boonson's astonishing 9.90-second dash proves that world-class results do not inherently require the newest technology or the most famous coaches. Sometimes, greatness requires only raw talent, a coach willing to patiently fine-tune the engine, and the historic grit of a gym that has been building champions for generations.
